main.title: World of Warcraft
main.subtitle: Azeroth Becomes a Place to Live Together
main.summary: Blizzard's shared world made routine, cooperation and long-term relationships part of an adventure.

cards.heading: An adventurer in a shared Azeroth
cards.text: World of Warcraft opened in North America, Australia and New Zealand on November 23, 2004. Blizzard turned the places, factions and history of Warcraft into a persistent online role-playing world. Players create an adventurer, undertake quests, learn professions and join other people for dungeons and longer journeys. Cities, roads and meeting places become familiar through repeated visits, while a character's progress continues across sessions. The people sharing that world give its routines much of their lasting appeal.

cards.heading: Familiar places and passing strangers
cards.text: Azeroth accommodates adventurers with different destinations. Along the same road, players encounter others fighting monsters, gathering resources, travelling or looking for a group. An inn becomes a meeting point and a capital becomes a place to trade or prepare for an expedition. Returning to these locations gives a session continuity with the last one. Familiar places matter because the player uses them regularly and shares them with other people.

cards.heading: Following the next quest
cards.text: Quests organise the journey through Azeroth. An exclamation mark identifies a character with a task; its description supplies objectives and a reward for completing them. Following those objectives introduces new places and helps a character grow. The journey still takes place among other players, so an encounter or a detour can change how it unfolds. This repeated cycle gives players a way to approach a large world one local task at a time.

cards.heading: Finding a party for the dungeon
cards.text: Dungeons bring different class abilities together. A warrior can hold an enemy's attention while a healer supports the party and other characters concentrate on damage. Players agree on a goal, travel to the same place and divide the work of surviving it. In the original game, arranging a group required more personal initiative than later automated systems. Repeated encounters helped establish acquaintances and reputations, one reason Blizzard treated the social experience as important when revisiting the game for World of Warcraft Classic.

cards.heading: A world drawn in strong silhouettes
cards.text: Strong silhouettes, exaggerated proportions and separated colours give Azeroth its recognisable appearance. In crowded areas, these choices help players distinguish creatures, characters and routes. The style also allowed the game to reach a broad range of PCs in 2004. Later graphical updates rebuilt many assets, but the emphasis on shape and colour kept the world visually familiar through those changes.

cards.heading: Learning where to look
cards.text: The original interface gives health, resources, abilities, targets, chat and inventory stable places on the screen. Action bars sit at the bottom, while portraits, indicators and a minimap provide other points of reference. With practice, a player learns where to check a cooldown or notice a party message during a fight. The number of things to watch can be daunting at first; their consistent placement helps turn them into habits.

cards.heading: The people who make a world familiar
cards.text: Guilds arrange regular play nights, players come to recognise names on their server, and the auction house supports a shared economy. These activities give the game a history made from its community's routines. Returning to an old meeting place can recall the people who once gathered there. World of Warcraft Classic revisited the original rules as well as the familiar scenery, including the effort involved in forming groups and building those relationships.

main.title: Dragon Quest VIII
main.subtitle: A familiar journey gains a visible horizon
main.summary: On November 27, 2004, Square Enix releases Dragon Quest VIII in Japan for PlayStation 2.

cards.heading: A familiar journey gains a visible horizon
cards.text: Square Enix released Dragon Quest VIII for PlayStation 2 in Japan on November 27, 2004. Developed with Level-5, it gives the series broad three-dimensional landscapes while retaining turn-based combat and Akira Toriyama's character designs. Roads, settlements and distant landmarks make travel visible at a new scale, with familiar battles and exploration organising the journey.

cards.heading: Roads through a three-dimensional world
cards.text: Hills, coasts and distant silhouettes let players see places before arriving. Routes invite detours and searches for landmarks, while settlements gain alleys and changes in height to explore. Moving through these spaces gives travel a physical scale, connecting the familiar sequence of towns, countryside and dungeons through a visible landscape.

cards.heading: Toriyama's designs in motion
cards.text: Cel shading and exaggerated proportions carry Toriyama's graphic style into moving models. Faces, colours and silhouettes remain clear during exploration and combat, and the monsters preserve the series' humorous character. The art direction gives its new three-dimensional figures continuity with the illustrations that had long defined Dragon Quest.

cards.heading: Tension, skills and alchemy
cards.text: Tension lets a character spend a turn building power for a later action. Skill points develop weapon categories and abilities, while the Alchemy Pot combines objects into equipment and consumables. These systems add preparation and timing decisions around the traditional battles, giving players several ways to approach a difficult opponent.

cards.heading: Level-5 works with a long-running series
cards.text: Level-5 brought PlayStation 2 RPG experience to the collaboration with Square Enix. The new presentation retains recurring monsters, straightforward menus and the series' humour. Familiar conventions give the broader environments a recognisable structure, making the change in scale part of an ongoing Dragon Quest journey.

main.title: Prince of Persia: Warrior Within
main.summary: Prince of Persia: Warrior Within is a 2004 action-adventure game developed and published by Ubisoft for GameCube, Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 2, and Xbox.

cards.text: Prince of Persia: Warrior Within is a 2004 action-adventure game developed and published by Ubisoft for GameCube, Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 2, and Xbox. It is the fifth main installment in the Prince of Persia series, and the sequel to 2003's Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time. A port for the PlayStation Portable developed by Pipeworks Software, titled Prince of Persia: Revelations, was released in 2005. Two mobile versions of Warrior Within were published by Gameloft for J2ME and iOS in 2004 and 2010, respectively. Due to issues with the in-game menu, the iOS version was temporarily pulled from the App Store for two weeks.

Set seven years after its predecessor, the game's story follows the Prince as he searches for a way to stop an entity called the Dahaka that is relentlessly pursuing him as punishment for his meddling with the Sands of Time. He travels to the mysterious Island of Time, where he attempts to prevent the Empress of Time from creating the Sands in the first place, hoping this act will appease the Dahaka.

Gameplay in Warrior Within builds upon that of The Sands of Time, adding new features, specifically options in combat. The Prince has the ability to wield two weapons at a time and to steal his enemies' weapons and throw them. The Prince's repertoire of combat moves has been expanded into varying strings that allow players to attack enemies with more complexity than was possible in the previous game. Warrior Within has a darker tone than its predecessor, adding in the ability for the Prince to dispatch his enemies with various gory finishing moves. In addition to the rewind, slow-down, and speed-up powers from The Sands of Time, the Prince also has a new sand power: a circular "wave" of sand that knocks down all surrounding enemies as well as damaging them.

Upon release, the game received generally positive reviews from critics, who singled out the improved combat, level design, story, and soundtrack. However, the radical shift in tone from its more light-hearted predecessor and the Prince's characterization garnered mixed reactions. Following Warrior Within, two more games set in The Sands of Time continuity were released: Prince of Persia: The Two Thrones in 2005, which is a direct sequel to Warrior Within; and Prince of Persia: The Forgotten Sands in 2010, set between The Sands of Time and Warrior Within.

main.title: WarioWare: Touched!
main.summary: WarioWare: Touched! is a 2004 action game developed by Nintendo SPD and Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo DS.

cards.text: WarioWare: Touched! is a 2004 action game developed by Nintendo SPD and Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo DS. The fourth installment of the WarioWare series, and the first of three on the Nintendo DS, the game involves rapidly completing "microgames" — simple minigames lasting extremely short periods of time — as quickly as possible. The microgames are exclusively controlled with the Nintendo DS's touchscreen and microphone.

The game was developed simultaneously with WarioWare: Twisted! The game was created to utilize the touchscreen functions of the Nintendo DS. WarioWare: Touched! was released in December 2004 in Japan, in February 2005 in both North America and Australia and in March of the same year in Europe. Touched! was a launch title for the Japanese, Australian, and European markets.

The game was positively received upon its release, with reviewers praising it for its fast-paced gameplay akin to other WarioWare titles, but disappointed by its brevity. Touched! introduced recurring character Ashley to the series and used the touchscreen and microphone for the first time. Many of the microgames in Touched! reappeared in WarioWare Gold. The game was re-released on the Wii U Virtual Console service in 2015 and briefly on the Nintendo 3DS the following year. The North American and Australian box arts are colored orange, while the box art for all the other regions are colored yellow.

main.title: Lumines
main.subtitle: A line turns a pattern into a beat
main.summary: Lumines lets a moving musical line decide when a finished visual pattern becomes a cleared space.

cards.heading: A puzzle to carry with headphones
cards.text: Lumines began on PSP in Japan on 12 December 2004, with North American and European releases following in 2005. Q Entertainment's puzzle used a portable screen and headphones as parts of one experience. Its coloured blocks, changing visual skins and music were designed to be encountered together.

cards.heading: A match waits for the line
cards.text: Falling two-by-two pieces contain two colours. Arranging their cells into larger matching squares prepares a group for removal, but a line moving with the music decides when that removal happens. Making a combination and waiting for it to clear are therefore separate parts of the same decision.

cards.heading: The player changes the sound
cards.text: Tetsuya Mizuguchi later described the original idea as a way to combine strong visuals, music and interaction on a machine carried like a personal music player. Actions add sounds aligned to the beat. A Remastered edition followed in 2018.

main.title: PlayStation Portable
main.subtitle: The screen leaves the living room
main.summary: Sony's first PlayStation handheld combines a widescreen display, UMD optical media and wireless connectivity.

cards.heading: Sony's first PlayStation handheld
cards.text:
The PlayStation Portable (PSP) is a handheld game console developed and marketed by Sony Computer Entertainment.

As a seventh generation console, the PSP mainly competed with the Nintendo DS.

cards.heading: The original PSP-1000 hardware
cards.text: The original PSP-1000 places a 4.3-inch widescreen between the controls, with a directional pad and analog nub on the left and PlayStation buttons on the right. Shoulder buttons extend its reach without obscuring the 480 × 272 display. A UMD drive sits behind the screen, while Memory Stick PRO Duo storage, USB and wireless networking give software and files other routes into the machine. At roughly 280 grams, its broad case combines a portable screen with a control layout recognisable to PlayStation players.

cards.heading: Games and films on UMD
cards.text: Sony chose UMD, a small optical disc protected by a shell, to offer more capacity than the solid-state media of the period. The format supports games with substantial audio and video data and was also proposed for films. Yet mechanical media bring energy costs, access times and moving parts into a handheld device. UMD becomes a symbol of PSP's ambition and compromise: it wants to bring living-room content into mobility, but carries it through technology that still resembles the world of home consoles.

cards.heading: Wireless links, music and video
cards.text: Its UMD format put games and films on small enclosed optical discs. Wireless networking offered local and online connections, while music and video playback gave the hardware uses beyond a single game. The broad screen, speakers and controls presented a compact entertainment device at a time when those jobs had not yet converged around the modern smartphone.

cards.heading: The widescreen display
cards.text: The 4.3-inch 16:9 screen immediately distinguished PSP from earlier handhelds. The format suited three-dimensional games, films and interfaces inspired by the wider Sony ecosystem. It also widened the body of the console and forced designers to reconsider text and HUD readability in mobile use. PSP shows that handheld quality is not only a matter of processor power. It depends on viewing distance, brightness, information density and the way hands coexist with a relatively large display.

cards.heading: LocoRoco and Patapon
cards.text: The machine's identity also came from games that suited its particular setting. LocoRoco and Patapon found different ways to organise movement, rhythm and attention on a portable screen. The PSP could carry familiar PlayStation worlds, but it also made room for experiences shaped around a different object in the player's hands.

main.title: Ridge Racer
main.summary: Ridge Racer, released in Japan as Ridge Racers, is a 2004 racing video game developed and published by Namco for the PlayStation Portable.

cards.text: Ridge Racer, released in Japan as Ridge Racers, is a 2004 racing video game developed and published by Namco for the PlayStation Portable. An installment in the Ridge Racer series, it was released as a global launch title for the system, on 12 December 2004 in Japan and overseas in 2005. Ridge Racer has been described as a 'compilation' of the series, featuring tracks, cars and remixed soundtrack from previous titles of the 1990s. Gameplay-wise, it marked the change from the "classic" style last seen in Ridge Racer V to the new drifting mechanic and nitrous boost that the series would incorporate from there on, including on Ridge Racer 6 and Ridge Racer 7.

Ridge Racer was critically acclaimed, praised for its visuals, gameplay and soundtrack; it was notable at the time for providing home console-like graphics at a smooth 60 fps framerate on a mobile gaming system, harnessing the PSP's graphical abilities. An updated version with more tracks and modes was released for the PSP in 2006 titled Ridge Racer 2; seven years after Ridge Racer on PSP came Ridge Racer on PlayStation Vita.

main.title: Metal Gear Acid
main.subtitle: Snake learns to plan a hand of cards
main.summary: Metal Gear Acid is Konami's PSP tactical stealth game, first released in Japan on 16 December 2004. It places Snake in an alternate story outside the main Metal Gear continuity, replacing continuous action with turns governed by a deck of cards. Movement, weapons and special actions depend on the hand available at that moment. The player recognises familiar equipment and characters, but uses them as parts of a plan. Its arrival on a handheld becomes an opportunity to reconsider how a stealth mission can be organised rather than simply reproduce the console games on a smaller screen.

cards.heading: Snake learns to plan a hand of cards
cards.text: Metal Gear Acid is Konami's PSP tactical stealth game, first released in Japan on 16 December 2004. It places Snake in an alternate story outside the main Metal Gear continuity, replacing continuous action with turns governed by a deck of cards. Movement, weapons and special actions depend on the hand available at that moment. The player recognises familiar equipment and characters, but uses them as parts of a plan. Its arrival on a handheld becomes an opportunity to reconsider how a stealth mission can be organised rather than simply reproduce the console games on a smaller screen.

cards.heading: A useful weapon can also be the next move
cards.text: Before a mission, the player prepares decks for the characters. During a turn, a card can be used for its particular effect or spent to move across the map. That choice gives an apparently valuable attack another possible purpose: it might be more important to reach cover now than preserve a weapon for later. A hand contains only a limited selection, so the intended plan must adapt to what has been drawn. The player balances the route through the area with the resources needed when an enemy finally has to be confronted.

cards.heading: A complete card game inside Metal Gear
cards.text: Shinta Nojiri directed and designed the project, with Nobuko Toda, Shuichi Kobori and Akihiro Honda composing the music. Cards draw on the wider Metal Gear series, making the deck a collection of recognisable references as well as a set of tactical tools. The game supplies its cards through normal play rather than requiring separate purchases. North American and European PSP releases followed in 2005, and a sequel arrived later that year in Japan. Acid's distinctive idea is to make preparation visible in the hand, where every possible action also competes with the need to move.

main.title: Donkey Kong Jungle Beat
main.summary: Donkey Kong Jungle Beat is a 2004 platform game developed and published by Nintendo for the GameCube.

cards.text: Donkey Kong Jungle Beat is a 2004 platform game developed and published by Nintendo for the GameCube. It follows the gorilla Donkey Kong as he sets out to defeat a series of evil kings to conquer the jungle. Jungle Beat is designed for use with the DK Bongos, a bongo drum-style GameCube controller created for the Donkey Konga (2003) rhythm game. The player controls Donkey Kong through various side-scrolling levels as he collects bananas, swings on vines, chains combos, rides animals, and defeats enemies and bosses.

The debut project of the 65-member Nintendo EAD Tokyo, Jungle Beat's development began around July 2003, after Shigeru Miyamoto suggested that Nintendo should commission a new Donkey Kong game. Development was led by director Yoshiaki Koizumi and producer Takao Shimizu, who sought to create a simple, accessible game in contrast to more complex contemporary games. Koizumi conceived a game that used the DK Bongos instead of a standard gamepad to control the player character, and applied lessons he had learned from previous projects during development. Because the tone differed from previous Donkey Kong games, the team excluded most of the franchise's existing elements and characters.

Jungle Beat was released in Japan in December 2004 and in the West in 2005 as the first major Donkey Kong game since Donkey Kong 64 (1999). It received mostly positive reviews from critics, who complimented its use of the DK Bongos, with praise for its visuals and level design, but was criticized for its short length and low difficulty level. Nintendo EAD Tokyo went on to develop the critically acclaimed Super Mario Galaxy (2007), which refined concepts that were introduced in Jungle Beat. Jungle Beat was rereleased as part of Nintendo's New Play Control! line of GameCube ports for the Wii in 2008; the port contains reworked controls and levels. This version was released as a downloadable game for the Wii U in 2016.

main.title: Cave Story
main.summary: Cave Story is a 2004 Metroidvania game developed by Daisuke "Pixel" Amaya.

cards.heading: Quote explores the caves
cards.text: Cave Story is a 2004 Metroidvania game developed by Daisuke "Pixel" Amaya. It was released on December 20, 2004 for Microsoft Windows. The game revolves around Quote, a robot who wakes up suffering from amnesia and explores diverse cavernous areas in order to uncover his backstory and escape from the cave. The character gains access to new areas as he powers up his weapons by collecting triangular experience crystals and solves various platforming puzzles. Quote speaks to non-player characters scattered around the game world in order to learn more about the world and its inhabitants. Cave Story features 2D platform mechanics and is reminiscent of the games Amaya played in his youth, such as Metroid and Castlevania.

cards.heading: A solo project reaches the wider industry
cards.text: After its initial self-published release, the game slowly gained popularity on the Internet. It received widespread critical acclaim for many polished aspects of its design, such as its compelling characters, setting, story, and gameplay. Cave Story is considered by many as one of the most influential video games of all time. It became an influence on indie games and the video game industry. Its polished design made a solo production visible alongside the work of much larger studios.

cards.heading: Ports, Cave Story+ and a 3D remake
cards.text: Independent video game developer Nicalis worked with Amaya to port the game to WiiWare and DSiWare in 2010. An enhanced version, Cave Story+, was released for Steam in November 2011, and the original game was released for the Nintendo 3DS in October 2012 with added content. A 3D remake of the game, titled Cave Story 3D, was developed by Nicalis and published by NIS America for the Nintendo 3DS in November 2011. A port of Cave Story+ for the Nintendo Switch was released in June 2017, with many visual enhancements. In 2026, the Steam version of the game was updated to more closely resemble the Switch version.
